notes: West leads the ♣K against 6♠. The only possible danger is a 4-1 heart break. South can guard against this possibility by playing for an elimination.

After winning the opening club lead, South should draw trump ending in the dummy. North's remaining club is ruffed in the closed hand. South now plays 3 rounds of diamonds ruffing the third round. Both clubs and diamonds have been eliminated and a trump remains in both the North and South hands.

South leads a low heart and when West follows low, a low heart is also played from North. East will win, but he will be endplayed. A heart return will allow South to pick up the suit and a minor suit return will concede a ruff and discard.

If West produces a heart honour on the first round of the suit, dummy plays low as before. If West began with only 1 heart, East can either duck, endplaying his partner, or overtake, endplaying himself.
If West started with 4 hearts to the ♥Q, ♥J, and ♥10, East will follow low leaving West endplayed. The contract is guaranteed by playing this way.

South's best chance is to cash 2 of North's diamonds and then revert to drawing the rest of East's trumps. On the last round of spades North's third diamond winner is discarded.
The diamonds are now unblocked and South can easily take the rest of the tricks.

Declarer should test diamonds first before playing on clubs. If diamonds do not break, South needs 4 club tricks. He should cash dummy's ♣K and plan to finesse the ♣J, playing for one of the following distributions: Distribution 1, Distribution 2, Distribution 3, Distribution 4. In the latter two cases, the first heart trick must have been won with the ♥A to preserve a later dummy entry.

If diamonds are 3-3, only 3 club tricks are needed. The club suit can always be played for 3 tricks by cashing the ♣A first and then playing the ♣8 through West, intending to run it if West follows low. If West has 4 clubs, there is nothing he can do. If East has 4 clubs, West will show out on the second round. South can rise with North's ♣K and lead towards the ♣J.

If West had started with guards in both spades and diamonds, the squeeze will operate with equal effectiveness. West will be squeezed on the play of the ♣A.

South should win the club lead and cash 3 more rounds of that suit. The ♦A should be cashed next, followed by a second diamond to the dummy. When diamonds prove to be 3-2 the contract is certain.

South cashes 1 more round of diamonds and leads a heart covering whatever East plays. West can win the trick cheaply, but he will be endplayed. Either a spade or a heart return will provide trick 12 for South.

Notice the importance of keeping a late diamond entry to the dummy. A spade return by West at the time of the endplay will give South a third spade trick, however, the suit will be blocked. Dummy's diamond entry will allow South to untangle the spades.

If West shows out on the second round of diamonds, the endplay will still work as above. If West turns up with 4 diamonds the elimination will no longer work as removing West's exit cards in diamonds will also remove dummy's entry to unblock the spades. South's best play will be to take 2 finesses, hoping East has either the ♠Q or the ♥K.

notes: South has 2 diamond losers and an almost certain loser in clubs as West's 2-level overcall must contain the ♣K. Dummy's third heart will provide a discard for 1 of these losers.

It may look tempting to duck the opening lead in attempt to rectify the count for a simple squeeze against West in clubs and diamonds. South could run his spade, diamond, and heart winners. On North's last heart, West will be forced to discard a diamond, making North's diamond high, or a club, allowing South to drop the ♣K.
The only problem with this plan is that West is very likely to have 6 diamonds. If allowed to win trick 1, West will be able to give East a diamond ruff.
South should win the opening lead and play his winners as before with the intention of strip squeezing West.

On dummy's last heart, West must discard a diamond in order to guard the ♣K. A diamond trick is now conceded to West forcing him to lead into South's club tenace. There may be ambiguity in the ending and South will likely have to guess West's remaining distribution.

The 2-suit strip squeeze is quite common. In this case, West was squeezed out of a surplus winner in diamonds so that he could be endplayed without being able to set the contract. This particular variety of strip squeeze matures with 2 or more losers.

notes: West leads the ♣K against 6NT. There are 11 top tricks (3 in spades, 4 in hearts, 3 in diamonds, and the ♣A). There are 2 chances. A defender (presumably East) might have started with 4 spades and a singleton club. He can be given a spade trick on the fourth round, establishing a long card for North.

South may also be able to squeeze West, if West has length in spades as well as clubs. There are 2 losers, but South cannot afford to duck the opening lead in an effort to rectify the count. West will switch to spades ruining the timing for the squeeze.
South can succeed by winning the ♣A and squeezing West without the count. South next runs his hearts and diamonds pitching a low spade from North on the penultimate winner.

West is squeezed when South leads his last winner. A spade discard gives up a trick immediately (a club is discarded from North). A club discard allows South to pitch a spade from North and give West a club trick, setting up a winner in the dummy.

South has to decide which opponent to play for length in spades. Both lines of play require winning the opening lead with the ♣A. South should next cash the hearts. When West has only 1 heart, he is a favourite to hold long spades and the squeeze without the count is the correct play.
When West has 2 hearts, the decision is close, but West should still be played for length in spades. When West has 3 or more hearts, East should be played for length in spades.

notes: West leads the ♠Q which South wins. South needs to play diamonds for 3 tricks. South's other 9 tricks will come from 2 spade tricks, 3 heart tricks, and 4 club tricks.
The only problem will occur when West started with all 4 diamonds. South should play a diamond to the ♦Q or ♦J early.
When East shows out South's only chance is to lead the ♦K at a point when West has only diamonds left. When South leads the ♦K West is held to 1 diamond trick no matter how he defends.

South will be able to squeeze the West hand down to all diamonds as long as West began with fewer than 5 clubs. South starts by cashing clubs. After the clubs are cashed, South may have to guess West's remaining major suit distribution and cash the suit that can be eliminated from West's hand.

South will usually have some idea as to which suit to play next from West's discards on the clubs. In the absence of any such information, hearts should next be played as there is 1 more winner in hearts than in spades. West is forced to pitch a spade on the third round of hearts.
South's remaining spade honour will strip West's last non-diamond. The ♦K can now be played forcing West to surrender.

NCA NCK NC2 SCQ SCJ SCT SC9

notes: West's heart opening lead should be won with the ♥A in dummy. South has no reason to duck this trick and a club shift might lead to a defensive ruff. South has a certain heart loser and must hold his trump losers to 2. Additionally, there might be trump control problems stemming from the blockage in clubs.
The best way to play spades for 2 losers is not very intuitive. South should lead a spade from dummy and, when East follows small, a low spade should be played by South.

All trump plays will succeed when trumps break 3-3. The contract is hopeless if trumps break 5-1. The only relevant 4-2 break that the suggested line loses to is West holding the ♠9 doubleton. All other lines do worse on the 4-2 breaks than the suggested line.

Low to the ♠J or ♠10 loses to a doubleton ♠K or ♠Q with West, twice as likely as ♠9 doubleton. Cashing the ♠A and leading a low spade loses to the ♠9 doubleton in either hand as well as West holding a small doubleton. Cashing the ♠A and leading the ♠J or ♠10 is worst of all. This play loses to doubleton honor in either hand as well as West holding a small doubleton.

When South makes the correct play of a low spade on the first round, West wins an honor and forces South to ruff a heart. South should continue trumps from the top, discarding dummy's blocking clubs. East will win the third round of trump and force South to ruff again. South can draw the last trump, discarding dummy's last club, and run the clubs.

By playing for an elimination, South can guarantee the contract. South should draw trump and play a diamond to dummy. Dummy's second club is ruffed and South exits in hearts.
A diamond play from either defender allows South to play that suit for 1 loser regardless of how diamonds lie. As a club return yields a ruff and discard, the defense must continue hearts.

South ruffs and plays a low diamond. When West follows small, South should duck in dummy. If East can win this trick, diamonds are breaking. If East discards, West is endplayed. He must either lead a diamond away from the ♦Q or give a ruff and discard by leading clubs.

notes: West's club opening lead is won in dummy. The contract will be easy if trumps are 3-2. If trumps are 4-1, South has two chances. He could either play to score his small trumps by ruffing dummy's clubs or play for a minor suit squeeze.

In either case, leading a club at trick 2 for a ruff in the closed hand is a good idea. If South is going to adopt the "squeeze line", ruffing a club will help to isolate the threat in that suit. If South is going to try to score all of his trumps, he must use each of dummy's 3 entries for club ruffs.

South should next cash the top trumps revealing that West began with a certain trump trick. South is now at the crossroads. If he chooses to play for a squeeze, he should surrender a trump trick at once. If East began with 4 or more diamonds along with 5 or more clubs, he can later be simple squeezed (or trump squeezed) on the run of the spades.

South gives himself slightly better odds, however, by playing to ruff all of dummy's clubs. West must have either 3415 or 3424 distribution for this line to succeed. South should begin by cashing 3 rounds of spades ending in the dummy. A second club is ruffed.

South cashes the ♦A and continues a low diamond. If West began with a singleton diamond, it will not help him to ruff (notice that if all of the spades had not been cashed earlier, West could defeat the contract by pitching a spade on the second diamond).
After dummy wins the ♦K, South leads dummy's last club and ruffs in the closed hand. West is forced to ruff his partner's diamond winner at trick 13.

The mathematics required to choose between the 2 lines of play are too complex for almost anyone to solve at the table. The odds of success of the 2 lines are very close but the "ruffing line" does give slightly better odds than the "squeeze line".

notes: West's club opening lead is won by South. The contract is in danger only if diamonds are 4-0. If West has 4 diamonds, the suit can be played for 2 losers provided that the ♦K is played on the first round.

It would be a mistake to play the ♦K at trick 2, however, as South would be left with no play when East holds all 4 diamonds. South does better by crossing to the ♥A and leading a diamond toward his ♦K.

It would be wrong to cross to dummy in spades (instead of hearts). Such a play would expose the closed hand to spade forces making it difficult or impossible to pick up 4 diamonds in West's hand for 2 losers.
When the ♦K holds as West discards, South's only hope of losing just 2 diamond tricks is to endplay East in trumps. There are 2 ways this might be accomplished.
If East is 3442, South can crossruff hearts and spades and lead a club in this position. East must ruff and lead away from his ♦A.

A better chance is to play clubs immediately. If clubs are 3-3, South should play East to be 3343. There are several possible winning sequences. For example, South can continue with the ♠A and a spade ruff. 2 rounds of hearts come next, dummy ruffing. Dummy's last spade is ruffed. South exits a low trump (or anything else) and East is held to 2 trump tricks as before.

If East turns up with 4 clubs, South should play East to be 3244. Again South has more than 1 winning line. For example, South can continue with the ♠A and a spade, ruffing. South's good club is ruffed. Dummy's last spade is ruffed and the ♥K is cashed. As before, East will be endplayed into giving up 1 of his trump tricks.

Spades are played next with East discarding on the second round. South cashes the ♣A and ♣Q. If both follow, or if East discards, clubs can be played for no losers and South will take at least 12 tricks.

If East happens to turn up with 4 clubs (unlikely since he also has 4 hearts), South cashes the ♣K and exits a club to East. East will be down to all diamonds and South will make the contract regardless of the location of the ♦K.

notes: West's lead of the ♣Q is taken by East with the ♣A. East returns a club, South winning the ♣K. South should be able to ruff his heart loser in the dummy but it cannot hurt to cash the ♠J first.
When West discards, the 5-0 break is revealed. Dummy's small spade now will be needed to finesse against East's ♠10. South will have to find another way to deal with his heart loser.

South should continue by drawing trump and cashing all of his major suit winners. The contract will make whenever diamonds are 2-2. South will also succeed when West has length in diamonds along with the remaining club honors (not unlikely given the lead). In this case West will be squeezed in the minors when South's last winner is cashed.
